newsitem.title: LEBANON: FEATURE - In Beirut, it's beauty and the bust.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - In Beirut, it's beauty and the bust.

text.p: At first, the 45-year-old grandmother had trouble persuading her husband it was worth $2,500 to help her fit in at Beirut's "Silicone Beach", where some women exhibit three different bikinis a day.
"Now my husband thinks my breast implants were the best investment he ever made," said the mother of four who frequents Beirut's thriving Riviera Beach, popular among women seeking bodily perfection.
Three of her friends followed suit, and a growing number of Lebanese women are concluding that breast implants -- and a host of other cosmetic procedures -- are a wise investment.
While the government pours billions of dollars into rebuilding war-ravaged Beirut, some of the most talked about reconstruction is on lips, thighs, noses -- and most notably -- beneath bikini tops.
Lebanon has always been the conservative Arab world's most liberal society. Women in miniskirts who would raise eyebrows in other Arab countries go almost unnoticed on the streets of Beirut.

As the country recovers from civil war, people are flaunting wealth ever more conspicuously -- from the largest Mercedes cars, to $1 million seaside apartments, to sculpting bodies at expensive health clubs, to cosmetic surgery.
Psychologists say beauty has become an addiction.
"My friends and I spend 90 percent of our time talking about it. It is driving us crazy," said Ramy, a computer engineer enjoying Riviera Beach.
BEAUTY CULTURE IS PERVASIVE
Some women are pleased with what nature provided. "We didn't need to do it," said Miralda, after she and her friend eyed a woman at the beach who had gone for a permanent pout.
But those not obsessed with good looks are bombarded with reminders that they should be.
Turn on your television in the morning and you find Haifa, a tall aerobics instructor who hosts a popular show called "There Is No Other Way But Haifa."
On the evening news, anchorwomen in low-cut blouses take you through world events. Female "meteorologists" in tight T-shirts follow with a review of the temperatures.
The beauty mania has sent many Lebanese to expensive, high-tech health clubs in search of the perfect figure, tan, nose, lips -- the list goes on.
At the recently opened $10 million underground Panacea club, beauticians recruited from Romania advise members in a sprawling cosmetic section.
Two floors down, customers on stairmasters and treadmills sweat off excess pounds while watching dancers gyrate on MTV's Grind show on a giant television screen.
PLASTIC SURGEONS ENJOY GROWING PROFITS
Those who miss the beauty train risk the wrath of jokes. While Riviera Beach is known as "Silicone Beach", nearby Coral Beach has been dubbed "Prostate Beach" for its older, unathletic crowd.
All the nose jobs, cellulite reduction, breast implants, lip jobs and face lifts are fattening the bank accounts of plastic surgeons, some of whom have returned after fleeing the civil war.
Plastic surgeons say breast implants pull in the biggest revenues, followed by nose jobs and the increasingly popular procedure that leaves a woman's lips in a permanent pout.

"Some women just want bigger breasts and others want to be bigger and better. Some are worried about their husbands playing around or looking elsewhere," said Dr Ibrahim Melki, who returned from the United States to open a practice.

Cosmetic surgeons apply the latest techniques -- from laser surgery to salt water breast implants -- there is no sign demand will ease anytime soon in a small country with more than 40 registered plastic surgeons.
One women who asked not to be named said years of aerobics and tennis three times a week were not enough. So she had her lips reshaped. One day, her husband came home to find her chest had grown.
"He told me I had guts," she said. "Nowadays women are open minded and understand the need to nourish the best parts of their bodies. It's contagious."
